Synopsis

Triada moved from an advanced Android trojan into the firmware supply chain for low-cost Android devices. Public reporting from Dr.Web, Google, and Kaspersky described variants embedded before sale, including a backdoored Android framework log function that could install modules from system context. The impact was deeper than an unwanted app: users received devices whose trusted base image could download payloads, display ads, install software, and survive normal removal.

Story

Triada began as a modular Android trojan that abused root privileges and tried to run inside core Android processes. Later variants moved into firmware images before sale. Users received devices that already contained the malware.

Google and Dr.Web described a preinstalled backdoor variant in which Android framework behavior was modified. The backdoored framework log path could load Triada code from system context, giving the malware privileged access to application installation and ad delivery. The device appeared new, but the base image was already compromised.

The suspected insertion point was not the Android Open Source Project itself. It was the commercial layer where device makers and partners customize firmware images before shipping. A factory reset does not remove malware from the system partition, and ordinary users cannot distinguish a clean build image from a compromised one.

This record keeps the early OEM/firmware-supply-chain Triada cases separate from the 2025 counterfeit-smartphone wave. They share malware lineage and tactics, but the public facts are different: older reports centered on legitimate low-cost device firmware and partner customization, while the later Kaspersky report described fake devices sold through online marketplaces.
